sections.title: Payout ceiling with a single operator output
notes: The miner was moved off the operator and the operator's wallet collapsed to a single 79999999000-unit output before measuring, because a wallet holding one coinbase output per block does not have this ceiling at all. The hub was stopped for the collapse and restarted into that wallet, which is what a freshly deployed hub holds.

The hub took 1 block(s) after restart to reach 24 spendable output(s). That is the fan-out's own cost and the one thing it makes worse: a wallet with a single output has nothing to pay from while the split is unconfirmed, so a cold hub cannot pay at all for one block. It is spent before the listener opens.

The `POST /faucet` latency here covers the whole flow -- challenge, solve, redeem -- and the stack runs the puzzle at 64 expected hashes. The pre-fix baseline timed a single payload-less POST against a hub that had no proof of work yet, so the two latency figures are not comparable and neither is evidence about the other.

754 payouts landed across 30 blocks (25.13 per block, 301.4 a minute, busiest block 26) against 1193 offered, with 439 refused for want of a funded output. §6.4b's one-per-block is refuted, which is the point: the operator's wallet is kept split across many confirmed outputs, so a payment always has one to spend and its change does not block the next.
